\section[il condominio]{il condominio — the block of flats; the joint ownership}

\label{lesson:IT-C449-condominio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the drain cover, then the Italian for to clutter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: il condominio}
\textbf{il condominio} — \textquotedblleft{}the block of flats; the joint ownership\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Nel nostro condominio ci sono venti famiglie.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There are twenty families in our block of flats.}
\end{quote}

\emph{La riunione di condominio} — the residents' meeting.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{condominio} is a learned borrowing from Modern Latin \emph{condominium} 'joint ownership' (EtymDB), built on \emph{dominium} 'ownership', from \emph{domus} 'house'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il condominio}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il condominio}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{il condominio}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for the drain cover, then the Italian for to clutter, then say \emph{il condominio} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does il condominio mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The block of flats; the joint ownership\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[l'impalcatura]{l'impalcatura — the scaffolding}

\label{lesson:IT-C449-impalcatura}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to clutter, then the Italian for the block of flats.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: l'impalcatura}
\textbf{l'impalcatura} — \textquotedblleft{}the scaffolding\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
C'è un'impalcatura davanti alla chiesa.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There is scaffolding in front of the church.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Il palco} — the stage, the platform.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{impalcatura} is built on \emph{palco} 'platform', which is usually traced to Lombardic \emph{balko} 'beam', a Germanic word that came into Italian as a borrowing.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{l'impalcatura}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{l'impalcatura}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for to clutter, then the Italian for the block of flats, then say \emph{l'impalcatura} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[la gru]{la gru — the crane (the machine and the bird)}

\label{lesson:IT-C449-gru}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the block of flats, then the Italian for the scaffolding.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la gru}
\textbf{la gru} — \textquotedblleft{}the crane (the machine and the bird)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Dalla finestra vedo una gru gialla.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{From the window I see a yellow crane.}
\end{quote}

Plural unchanged: \emph{le gru}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{gru} is inherited from Latin \emph{grus} 'crane' (EtymDB); the machine is named after the bird's long neck.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[crollare]{crollare — to collapse}

\label{lesson:IT-C449-crollare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the scaffolding, then the Italian for the crane.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: crollare}
\textbf{crollare} — \textquotedblleft{}to collapse\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Il vecchio ponte è crollato.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The old bridge collapsed.}
\end{quote}

Also figurative: \emph{sono crollato dal sonno} — I dropped off to sleep.

\begin{cousinweb}
The origin of \emph{crollare} is not settled; it first meant to shake.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[sgomberare]{sgomberare — to clear (out), to evacuate}

\label{lesson:IT-C449-sgomberare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the crane, then the Italian for to collapse.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sgomberare}
\textbf{sgomberare} — \textquotedblleft{}to clear (out), to evacuate\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Hanno sgomberato la strada dopo la frana.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{They cleared the road after the landslide.}
\end{quote}

Also \emph{sgombrare}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sgomberare} is built from \emph{s-} and the root of \emph{ingombrare} 'to clutter': to take the clutter away. The origin of that root is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{sgomberare}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for the crane, then the Italian for to collapse, then say \emph{sgomberare} again
\end{itemize}
